In this paper, we theoretically investigate the generalization behavior of Transformer-based neural quantum states under ICL. By establishing a rigorous inference-time generalization error bound, we show that the prediction error decreases inversely with both the number of in-context examples and the depth of the Transformer architecture. Our analysis further demonstrates that achieving such guarantees requires a Transformer depth that scales linearly with the system size, measured either by the number of particles in continuous systems or the number of qudits in discrete systems. Furthermore, our results provide a quantitative characterization of how in-context information can be exploited at inference time to improve prediction accuracy, offering a principled perspective on data-dependent generalization in neural quantum state representations. Taken together, these findings contribute to a theoretical understanding of ICL in quantum many-body modeling and highlight the scalability of Transformer-based architectures in high-dimensional quantum systems. Numerical experiments further support our theoretical predictions and confirm the derived scaling laws.






A number of theoretical questions remain open. The present analysis is established through an augmented embedding construction that facilitates the proof, whereas the numerical experiments are conducted using the practical embedding matrix. Although the empirical results exhibit the same scaling behavior under the practical embedding, extending the current theoretical framework to rigorously analyze this practically relevant setting remains an important direction for future research. Moreover, an important direction is to identify assumptions that are intrinsic to quantum learning problems, thereby replacing the current proof-oriented assumptions with conditions that more precisely capture the underlying quantum structure. Finally, while the present work establishes the existence of Transformer architectures achieving the desired inference-time generalization guarantees, it remains an important open question whether practical training algorithms can be shown to converge to such solutions with provable guarantees.

Conclusions




We have investigated the emergence of a chaotic Griffiths phase in networks of coupled map-based neurons, focusing on the role of quenched heterogeneity in the local dynamics. In contrast with previous studies in which Griffiths phases have been primarily associated with structural disorder, our results show that topological heterogeneity is not necessary for the emergence of a chaotic Griffiths phase. In a globally coupled network of Chialvo maps, quenched disorder in a local neuronal parameter is sufficient to produce an extended intermediate regime between desynchronized and coherent chaotic dynamics. Moreover, the chaotic Griffiths phase is absent for identical neurons and progressively broadens as the degree of local parameter heterogeneity increases, establishing a direct connection between intrinsic dynamical diversity and the emergence of extended critical behavior.






The chaotic Griffiths phase is characterized by the intermittent formation and destruction of neuronal clusters and large temporal fluctuations in the fraction of clustered neurons. The cluster-size distributions exhibit power-law behavior over a finite interval of coupling strengths, with exponents that vary with the coupling parameter. These results provide evidence that the observed intermittent regime represents extended critical behavior rather than a conventional transition occurring at an isolated critical point.






We have also explored the combined effects of intrinsic and structural heterogeneity by considering Chialvo maps with heterogeneous local parameters coupled through a small-world network. The introduction of topological disorder substantially extends the range of coupling strengths over which the chaotic Griffiths phase occurs and prevents the system from reaching the coherent regime over the parameter interval investigated. Power-law cluster-size distributions persist throughout this enlarged region. Thus, local dynamical heterogeneity and structural disorder provide distinct but complementary mechanisms for sustaining extended critical behavior.

title: Divide and conquer: Scalable performance and energy in MCM GPUs
hypothesis: This limited understanding leaves industry and research without clear guidance on the performance and energy trade-offs of MCM GPU scaling. In this work, we investigate whether distributing compute and memory capability across multiple chiplets offers a more scalable alternative to concentrating resources.
conclusion:
Conclusions




This work demonstrates our initial divide and conquer hypothesis, confirming that disaggregation is an effective architectural strategy for improving the scalability, performance, as well as energy consumption and efficiency of MCM GPUs. However, its benefits depend not only on increasing the number of chiplets, but also on, the scalability strategy and providing an interconnection network capable of sustaining the resulting communication demands.






Our systematic evaluation of scale-up, scale-out, and hybrid strategies shows that network scalability becomes the primary determinant of performance as chiplet count increases. Increasing the number of SMs or memory controllers in isolation provides limited benefits when inter-chiplet bandwidth, and contention constrain resource utilization. In contrast, highly scalable topologies enable disaggregated configurations to surpass equivalent monolithic designs, even beyond the current four-chiplet industry standard.






The results indicate that compute, memory, and interconnect resources must be co-designed and scaled jointly. Among the evaluated configurations, the 16 chiplet Torus with 256 SMs, representative of next-generation GPUs, provides the most balanced design point, delivering 
2.40
×
2.40\times

4.45
×
4.45\times
.
Further disaggregation can yield additional efficiency gains when supported by an adequate network.






Overall, these findings establish disaggregation and interconnect scalability as first-order considerations in MCM GPU design and provide practical architectural guidance for developing scalable, high-performance, and energy-efficient next-generation GPUs. Future work will extend this study by exploring adaptive routing mechanisms, evaluating heterogeneous interconnects that combine different link capabilities, and developing advanced data-placement algorithms to improve locality and reduce inter-chiplet communication.

title: When Numbers Start Talking: Numerical Signalling and Strategic Behaviour Among LLMs
hypothesis: We observe that structured messages alter the final payoffs for most games and LLMs, but without a predictable pattern; this challenges the assumption that AI agents can converge to stable equilibria regardless of additional capabilities. In this work, we study the effect of communication between AI agents in shaping the outcome of strategic games, with a particular focus on the formation of cooperation. We seek to understand the different effects that verbal and non-verbal communication may have on the emergence of cooperative behaviour in strategic games, depending on the LLM family and the agents’ assigned personality.
conclusion:
Conclusion




We investigated how non-verbal and poorly interpretable communication affects coordination among AI agents, examining message structure, receiver-side associations, and cooperation outcomes across four canonical games and four LLM families. At the symbolic level, instructed numerical signalling follows a shared regularity: all four LLMs concentrate decimal signals on compact, payoff-anchored symbol sets, and repetition consolidates these conventions. At the behavioural level, no comparable regularity emerges, as the strategic effect of signalling depends on each model’s prior. Our results do not establish a shared semantic code but show that bare instructions suffice for numerical messages to become structured, receiver-sensitive, and reinforced by repetition. Restricting natural-language communication alone is therefore unlikely to prevent structured numerical signalling in LLM-based MAS: monitoring should prioritise message-level fingerprints, particularly the within-model entropy gap to a true random baseline, which generalises across models, over behavioural signatures, which do not.






Several design choices bound these conclusions. We studied 
instructed
, not spontaneous, signalling, i.e., a lower bound on channel capacity rather than evidence of emergent covert coordination. Personalities are limited to two fixed types, payoffs are canonical, the repeated horizon is known, decoding follows provider defaults (so only within-model entropy gaps are portable across models), and within-round messages follow a fixed, non-counterbalanced order. The receiver test establishes sensitivity to message features, not shared semantics, and trajectory correlations rest on at most eight series per mode, so channel orderings are descriptive.






Overall, communication, even when non-verbal, can alter the coordination capabilities of AI-based MAS in model-dependent ways, with consequent risks for their interpretability, portability, and fairness. Since these effects emerge from mutual interactions rather than from model scaling alone, future work should investigate uninstructed signalling and system-level mechanisms that mitigate emergent risks as AI-MAS reach real-world deployment.

This paper studied the secrecy performance of a cooperative SWIPT-NOMA system with AN-aided relaying under practical impairments. In the considered system, the source employs OSTBC transmission, legitimate users adopt RAS, and the EVE applies MRC. The effects of CEEs, FBD, ipSIC, and imperfect AN cancelation are incorporated into the analysis to reflect practical transmission conditions. 
Analytical SOP expressions and high-SNR secrecy characterizations

The analytical results are verified by Monte Carlo simulations, showing a close agreement between theory and simulation. The results demonstrated that the proposed scheme benefits from both transmit diversity provided by OSTBC and receive diversity provided by RAS. Increasing the OSTBC order and the number of receive antennas at the legitimate users improves the secrecy performance, whereas increasing the number of EVE antennas degrades it due to the enhanced combining capability of EVE. It is also shown that the AN power allocation factor has a significant effect on the system performance. An appropriate choice of 
λ
\lambda

Under ideal 
CSI

In contrast, under practical impairments, the SOP curves converge to non-zero error floors, which indicates that residual interference and channel uncertainty limit the achievable secrecy performance. In particular, ipSIC causes noticeable degradation for the users performing SIC, while imperfect AN cancelation and outdated/erroneous channel information further reduce the secrecy reliability. The results also showed that proper allocation of AN power can alleviate the performance loss caused by additional EVE antennas and improve both secrecy throughput and SEE.
Overall, the considered OSTBC/RAS-based SWIPT-NOMA system with relay-generated AN provides an effective framework for enhancing physical-layer security in energy-constrained cooperative networks. The MLCommons Jailbreak Benchmark v1.0 provides the first complete end-to-end execution of the MLCommons jailbreak benchmarking methodology. Discussion




The results obtained in this work highlight the fundamental role played by the interaction between spatial structure and local rumor dynamics in determining the long-term behavior of stochastic spreading processes. Although the three models considered here share the same underlying transmission mechanism, they exhibit remarkably different qualitative behaviors. In particular, the presence or absence of mechanisms that remove active spreaders from the rumor front leads to substantially different phase diagrams. The classical Maki–Thompson model becomes extinct for every transmission rate, whereas the introduction of forgetting mechanisms gives rise to genuine phase transitions between extinction and survival. This contrast demonstrates how subtle modifications of local interaction rules can produce significant changes in the global behavior of spatial stochastic systems.






Our analysis shows that, in one dimension, the linear geometry of the lattice imposes strong constraints on the propagation of the rumor, and the interactions occurring near the expanding boundary play a crucial role in determining whether the process can sustain long-range growth. For the 
CRS
 model, the quadratic growth of the critical transmission rate for large stifling rates suggests that the main obstruction to survival arises from repeated stifling events occurring at the rumor frontier. The heuristic argument based on parent–child interactions indicates that this suppression mechanism is not merely a local phenomenon but is amplified by the spatial organization of the process, leading to the observed scaling behavior.






The comparison between the 
CRS
 and 
MT

Although both models incorporate forgetting and admit survival for sufficiently large transmission rates, their critical curves exhibit distinct asymptotic regimes. In the 
MT

α
\alpha

These observations emphasize that the microscopic details of the interaction rules, rather than only macroscopic parameters such as transmission and forgetting rates, are essential in determining the emergence of phase transitions.






Several interesting questions remain open even in the one-dimensional setting considered here. A natural direction is the rigorous investigation of the monotonicity properties of survival probabilities with respect to the model parameters, as well as a more detailed comparison between the different rumor mechanisms. Establishing ordering relations between the models and determining sharper asymptotic properties of the critical curves represent challenging mathematical problems that may provide further insight into the role of local interactions in spatial spreading processes.






Beyond one dimension, the present results suggest several avenues for future research. Extending these models to higher-dimensional lattices would allow the investigation of how the geometry of the rumor frontier influences critical behavior and survival mechanisms. Similarly, the study of tree-like structures and heterogeneous networks may reveal how branching effects and complex connectivity patterns compete with local extinction mechanisms. Such extensions could provide a bridge between rigorous results for spatial stochastic systems and the analysis of information spreading phenomena in realistic networks.






Finally, the numerical results obtained in this work illustrate the value of combining rigorous probabilistic methods with computational approaches in the study of critical phenomena. Exact continuous-time simulations provide access to parameter regimes where analytical techniques become challenging, while theoretical arguments help identify the mechanisms underlying the observed scaling laws. This interplay between analysis and computation offers a promising framework for further investigations of phase transitions in stochastic models of information spreading.

Conclusion




Stablecoins sit at the intersection of public blockchains, traditional finance, cross-chain infrastructure, and regulation. Their concentrated issuer, custody, oracle, bridge, and upgrade controls make them unusually sensitive to a CRQC, while their host-chain, rollup, and privacy dependencies prevent any one actor from completing the migration alone. The central stablecoin-specific problem is the authority–liability gap: the party able to change a component is often different from the users, exchanges, protocols, or issuers that bear the loss if it fails.






A practical transition should begin with a function-level cryptographic inventory, protect issuer-controlled infrastructure, add contract, bridge, and oracle safeguards, adopt host-chain signature agility, and define explicit treatment of dormant and wrapped supply. Standardized KEMs and signatures provide necessary building blocks, but do not by themselves replace aggregate bridge attestations, threshold custody, private and compliance-enabled transfers, rollup proofs, or recovery governance. Regulation further constrains the result by requiring continuity of redemption, reserve control, audit evidence, and intervention capabilities.






The research agenda is therefore compositional. It includes complete-operation benchmarks, formal models of layered residual risk and migration authority, efficient aggregate and threshold authorization, post-quantum privacy and compliance mechanisms, protocols for dormant balances and legacy wrapped routes, and empirical measurement of quantum-vulnerable stablecoin supply. Progress should be measured not by whether one key has been replaced, but by whether authorization, redemption, supply integrity, finality, privacy, and legally required controls remain valid across the full stablecoin system.

In this work, our primary focus has been to demonstrate the potential of augmenting nanophotonic devices with programmable nonlinearity. We believe one of the most important contributions of our work is to point toward a new development and manufacturing paradigm beyond the conventional one-device-one-function approach, which could eventually enable truly scalable integrated nonlinear photonics. A programmable device can be deployed as a “blank slate” that then inversely designs its own function, in situ, based on real-time feedback from the environment in which it operates. This would not only enable the robust engineering of complex functions with 100% yield but also allow the device to remain fully adaptive to changing environments and demands, potentially transcending nonlinear nanophotonics beyond its present regime of small circuit depths toward systems of much greater scale.






As the technology matures, the exact means of realizing programmable nonlinearity may well evolve. Our approach based on a photoconductor and free-space programming illumination was convenient for a proof of concept, but to maximize integrability, it may turn out to be advantageous to employ lithographically defined electrodes and integrated circuitry to control the bias electric fields. In analogy with the transistor, this large market could justify the extensive manufacturing and design optimization that might be prohibitive for more specialized nonlinear nanophotonic devices. This work aims to develop an AI-based building management system with two main components. The first automates AI algorithm deployment to manage load fluctuations by integrating dynamic SLAs. We propose using the established open-source FIWARE standard to decouple SLA management. This is necessary as the Kubernetes-based scheduler remains a closed system, accessible through FIWARE.






We have developed and tested two online AI algorithm examples that are foundational to machine learning and useful in the context of smart buildings. The key challenge is to create memory-efficient solutions for our microcontroller library. Our solutions apply to the ARDUINO ecosystem, and some algorithms are also designed for the Micropython ecosystem, another platform for microcontroller programming.






Regarding the development aspect of our work, limitations include a time lag between ecosystem algorithm developments (ARDUINO and Micropython), an incomplete understanding of online algorithms for building management, and the need for feedback on additional datasets.






More generally, it’s important to revisit the assumptions underlying this work, which some may disagree with. For example, we assumed that the cloud orchestrator was ultimately a black box that we didn’t control. Therefore, the orchestrator is assumed to run in a private cloud that we don’t own.






On the other hand, we assumed that the SLA management module, using FIWARE, which is open source (for the part we’re interested in), could be deployed within the building, along with the measurement sensors. The "building is the data center" approach is, in our case, somewhat loose. We could very well use a cloud orchestrator that would also be deployed within the building. Furthermore, on the downside, we believe our proposal is less suitable for a situation where we need to train a general model (in the machine learning sense) for all buildings. This paper outlines our perspective and recent progress towards developing a decentralized system that learns from real-time building data to support smart and sustainable environments with a focus on privacy. We propose treating the building itself as the data hub, adhering to edge computing concepts to protect privacy and lessen dependence on external cloud services.






This is especially important in humanitarian settings, where data ownership, energy conservation, and infrastructure limitations are crucial. We describe a lightweight orchestration framework akin to "Kubernetes" for the deployment of AI services within these environments and exhibit our advances in applying AI algorithms on low-power, affordable microcontrollers, such as those in the Arduino ecosystem. By facilitating on-site learning directly on sensors or microcontrollers, our initiative aims to introduce intelligent services to resource-constrained settings, enhancing autonomy, resilience, and sustainable growth in vulnerable or underserved communities.

This section discusses design choices and tradeoffs beyond GridSMR’s core architecture.






0.E.1 
System-Level Optimizations




Pipelining and Continuous Execution




The protocol description presents execution sequentially for clarity, but the system can be pipelined in practice.
Within blocks, many activations are independent due to the execution model and can execute in parallel at both leaders and followers.
The key constraint is maintaining determinism and causality through correct timestamp computation and clear block boundaries.
Assuming each shard hosts multiple accounts, followers can interleave and parallelize execution across accounts within the same shard while preserving the required per-account execution order.








Long-Running Activations




In GridSMR, an activation’s execution need not complete within a single block interval.
Unlike traditional blockchains that use commit-then-execute, where consensus determines the order of transactions before execution begins,
GridSMR’s execute-before-agree pattern decouples execution duration from block timing.






The fundamental challenge in commit-then-execute systems is that consensus commits to a specific set of transactions for each block without knowing their execution time.
Once block 
k
k
 is committed, all transactions in that block must execute to completion before the system can proceed to block 
k
+
1
k+1
.
If any transaction takes too long to execute, the system stalls waiting for it to complete.
This forces a bound on per-transaction execution, typically enforced through gas limits or execution time caps.






GridSMR relaxes this constraint because execution happens before consensus, and blocks are determined “retroactively” by the leader clock.
The leader executes activations continuously and periodically packages completed work into blocks for consensus.
If an activation does not complete before a block boundary, it is included in a later block, once its execution completes.
The activation is tagged with that block identifier, ensuring any continuations it spawns inherit the correct minimum block id for causal ordering.






Per-activation computation remains bounded – activations are gas-metered against a declared maximum – but that bound need not fit within a block interval.










0.E.2 
Policy and Mechanism Choices




Fairness Mechanisms




Blockchains often aim to provide fairness to users through mechanisms such as rotating leaders or restrictions intended to mitigate MEV attacks
such as front-running and sandwich attacks 
[
9
, 
26
]
.
Fairness is not the focus of this paper.
However, removing atomicity at the infrastructure level permits additional interleavings across activation trees.
A malicious leader may therefore reorder continuations from concurrent activation trees, potentially violating application-level ordering expectations.






Applications requiring ordering guarantees beyond GridSMR’s default per-account execution order can introduce application-specific coordination.
For example, an application can designate a specific account as a 
synchronizer
 through which relevant continuations are ordered before further execution.
Such synchronization reduces parallelism for the affected execution paths, but allows applications to selectively obtain stronger ordering guarantees when needed.








Follower Verification Strategies




The follower verification protocol divides verification into two phases: executing activations in the proposal, then verifying continuations.
A coordination mechanism is needed to allow shards to transition from phase one to phase two, ensuring the first phase has completed across all shards in the cluster.
Without this coordination, a shard might begin continuation verification before other shards have sent their continuations, leading to false rejection of valid blocks.






Our implementation uses standard timeout techniques, but alternative approaches exist.
For example, the cluster representative could collect completion signals from shards and coordinate the phase transition.
This approach can identify Byzantine proposals in some scenarios but requires additional synchronization within the cluster during phase two of follower execution.

Questions about the distribution of consciousness cannot be resolved by
direct observation alone. Because subjective experience is directly
accessible only in the first person, inferences about consciousness in
other entities must rely in part on analogy. Our central claim is that
not all analogies are equally informative: the evidential force of an
analogy depends primarily on similarity in factors that are plausibly
involved in generating consciousness, rather than on similarity in
downstream behavioural or cognitive effects.






This distinction helps explain why the human analogy supports

consciousness in current AI systems. Across biological species,
evolutionary continuity, shared physiology and convergent functional
organization provide at least some basis for causal comparison with the
human case. By contrast, although contemporary AI systems exhibit
impressive behavioural similarity to humans, their correspondence to the
candidate mechanisms currently thought to underlie human consciousness

limited support for attributing consciousness to present AI.






At the same time, weak analogical support from the human case should not
be confused with proof of impossibility. Artificial consciousness could
in principle arise through a different mechanism, substrate, or
organizational route. The key scientific challenge, therefore, is not
simply to ask whether AI behaves like us, but to identify what kinds of
evidence would justify claims about consciousness in any non-human
system. Progress will depend on clarifying the causal basis of
consciousness in humans, improving comparative evaluation across animal
taxa, and developing principled criteria for assessing genuinely

CONCLUSION




Sign language machine translation sits at a unique intersection of computer vision, linguistics, and deaf community perspectives. This manuscript has examined the landscape from multiple perspectives, highlighting both achievements and persistent gaps. The field has evolved from early rule-based and gloss-dependent systems toward end-to-end SLT and SLP pipelines. Recent work has demonstrated the effectiveness of pose-based representations, transformer architectures, and self-supervised learning. Large language models have been successfully integrated into SLT pipelines, improving fluency and semantic coherence. For SLP, advances in neural rendering and diffusion models have enabled higher-fidelity generation. These developments reflect both architectural innovation and the growing availability of large-scale datasets from broadcast and web sources.






Despite this growth, a disconnect remains between what systems achieve on benchmarks and what they deliver in practice. While dataset scale has increased, most large-scale data consists of broadcast interpretations rather than conversational signing, and annotation remains costly. The metrics used to measure progress tell us whether output matches a reference, but not whether it would be understood or accepted by a deaf user.
These gaps point toward where future effort is needed. Model architectures must better account for the linguistic properties, particularly simultaneity, spatial grammar, and non-manual marking, which remain poorly modeled or ignored entirely. Reducing dependence on expensive gloss annotations through self-supervised and weakly-supervised methods would enable learning from larger and more diverse data sources. Evaluation frameworks should better capture translation quality, potentially through human evaluation protocols or learned metrics that account for sign language structure. Investigation of domain adaptation and few-shot learning are needed to improve generalization across signers and contexts.






None of this can happen in disciplinary isolation. Modeling decisions benefit from linguistic insight; evaluation gains validity when deaf signers assess output quality; data collection becomes more ethical when communities shape governance from the outset. The technical challenges are not purely engineering problems awaiting algorithmic solutions; they are sociotechnical challenges whose resolution requires sustained collaboration across computer vision, linguistics, and deaf communities. Systems that achieve high scores but produce signing that deaf users find unnatural or incomprehensible have not solved the sign language machine translation problem–they have merely optimized for the wrong objective. A community-informed approach offers not only ethical grounding but methodological correction: by centering the perspectives of those who will use these systems, researchers can better identify which problems matter and what success actually looks like.

title: Long-Range Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Defect Energetics in SrTiO$_3$
conclusion:
Conclusion




Overall, we have presented a systematic benchmark of long-range machine learning interatomic potentials, namely MACE-LES, MACE-POLAR, and LOREM, progressing from idealised synthetic point-charge systems to DFT data for strontium titanate with Sr–O Schottky vacancy pairs.






In the synthetic benchmark, MACE-LES emerged as the strongest performer, demonstrating that explicit long-range energy evaluation in reciprocal space confers a meaningful advantage when the interaction is purely electrostatic. In the DFT data benchmark, all three long-range models showed strong generalisation across training regimes, producing correctly shaped and quantitatively reliable minimum energy pathways for oxygen vacancy migration, yielding activation barriers in good agreement with literature values. This is a notable extrapolation, as the training data comprised only bulk MD configurations and relaxed (endpoint) Schottky defect structures, with no intermediate migration geometries resembling the transition-state configurations sampled along the NEB path. By contrast, purely short-range models such as standard MACE remain fundamentally limited by their real-space cutoff, and this limitation becomes especially acute in defected structures where charged defects introduce slowly decaying electrostatic interactions.






However, there exist several important caveats with these findings. The synthetic benchmark, while instructive for isolating electrostatic behaviour, is by design an extreme test case: few real materials present interactions as purely long-range as formal point charges, and a model’s underperformance on this task should not be taken as disqualification for most applications. Similarly, the DFT benchmark metrics should not be interpreted as straightforward improvements over the synthetic case. The complexity of the DFT total energy, encompassing short-range repulsion, exchange-correlation, dispersion, and ionic self-energies, dilutes the electrostatic signal and could reduce the associated errors with electrostatics.






Looking forward, several extensions of this work can be considered. Phonon calculations and the evaluation of finite-temperature thermodynamic properties would test whether the long-range accuracy demonstrated in static benchmarks carries through to dynamical quantities. More complex defect structures, including higher vacancy concentrations and non-neutral supercells with explicit compensating charges, would probe the models’ robustness under conditions directly relevant to electrochemical applications such as solid-state batteries, where the repeated insertion and removal of ions leaves residual charge in the electrode material. Finally, a broader survey of strongly polar and ionic materials beyond SrTiO
3
 would establish the degree to which these conclusions generalise across the wider space of oxide and halide compounds where long-range electrostatics plays a central role.

Discussion




In the previous section, we summarized students’ perceptions of the system: whether they could accurately assess system performance, when they were able to make progress, when they became stuck or diverted, and how their confidence changed. Here, we examine what explains these results. We distinguish findings that stem from current technical limitations from findings shaped by formally verified languages’ properties and our design choices. We then discuss design implications for future formally verified co-reasoning (FVCR) systems, including the limitation of formal languages, the design strategies that may address them, and the open challenges that remain. Table 
1
 summarizes five capabilities that a co-reasoning system may need and compares our system with the support provided by an LLM-based assistant and a formal debugger.






9.1. 
What results stem from technical limitations?




LeanSide was developed under the cost constraints of a classroom deployment, so each verification was optimized for responsiveness and resource use. Recent commercial auto-formalizers 
(
Achim et al., 2025
)
 report higher success rates in generating compiling proofs for correct Lean statements. Plugging stronger models into the pipeline would likely improve accuracy by reducing false negatives, and may also slightly reduce unfaithfulness. By contrast, we do not expect stronger provers to substantially change error-message understandability or most student behaviors around making progress or getting stuck, as these are more closely tied to the nature of formal verification and our system design choices.








9.2. 
What could an FVCR system provide?




We view an FVCR system like LeanSide could contributes four resources to a human-AI co-reasoning system: preserving the user’s reasoning path, providing low-false-positive validity checks, producing hallucination-free reasoning feedback, and helping users iteratively make implicit reasoning explicit.






First, our findings show that LeanSide can help 
preserve user agency through faithful representation
. Although we observed edge cases where the system unfaithfully auto-corrected step-level mistakes, LeanSide usually followed the user’s reasoning at the user’s granularity. This was not due to formal verification alone, but our system design choice for step-by-step auto-formalization. Prior work in human-AI collaboration has shown that LLM outputs can introduce useful directions, but can also unintentionally distract users from their original initiative 
(
Jakesch et al., 2023
; 
Levy et al., 2021
)
. Plausible but misaligned outputs can pull users away from their original line of reasoning, forcing them to monitor and repair the system or follow its suggested direction 
(
Subramonyam et al., 2024
; 
Mozannar et al., 2024
; 
Cros Vila and Sturm, 2025
)
. An FVCR system can reduce this risk by designing the system to always follow the user’s reasoning path. In our system, the unit of preservation is the pre-processed smallest progression unit: we do not require the system to preserve lower-level decompositions inside that unit. This unit is context-dependent and can be customized to the reasoning task. For example, in a tax-reasoning system, the unit might be one claimed inference: given a taxpayer’s income, deductions, filing status, or transaction history, the system would preserve the user’s intended application of a specific tax rule and then verify whether the stated tax consequence follows.






Second, our findings also shows an FVCR system can help 
localize errors through low-false-positive feedback
. Hallucination remains a persistent concern in high-stakes reasoning domains. LLM feedback can be unreliable in these settings because it may sound plausible while being logically wrong 
(
Kim et al., 2025
; 
Bo et al., 2025
; 
Spatharioti et al., 2025
)
. A formally verified backend can instead provide a stronger basis for accepting a step or conclusion when the translation is faithful. In our system, verified steps helped students narrow down the issue: once a step was verified, students gained confidence in its validity and could focus on unverified steps to correct faulty logic or fill the gaps. This process continued until all steps were verified, or until students used their mathematical knowledge to judge that a remaining unverified step reflected prover failure rather than their own error, as described in Section 
7.2
.






Third, an FVCR system can provide 
verified reasoning suggestions
. In our system, these traces appeared as continuation hints and as informal comments in the Lean code panel explaining how a step was proved. Both were natural-language explanations grounded in verified reasoning, and both were proven to be useful to students. Similar opportunities may arise in other reasoning tasks where users need more than a validity check mark: they also need natural-language explanations of why a step follows.






Finally, an FVCR system can help users make 
implicit reasoning explicit
. In our study, students often entered high-level or ambiguous reasoning, while the system returned less ambiguous informalizations at the user’s granularity. By comparing their input with these interpretations, students could notice ambiguity, clarify assumptions, and make their reasoning more rigorous. This suggests that formal verification can serve not only as a checker, but also as a mirror for helping users refine high-level strategies into precise reasoning.








9.3. 
LeanSide Limitations, and Design Implications for Future FVCR Systems




LeanSide was designed to isolate how formal language can support students’ proof iteration. Some of its limitations therefore come from deliberate design choices, which could help explain why students became stuck or diverged.






First, Lean error messages can reflect 
overly-granular reasoning
, which can confuse users. The limited understandability of step-level error messages illustrates this limitation. When students wrote a statement as a single assertion, they often treated it as not requiring further explanation in the course context. Lean errors, however, often reflected failures in lower-level proof obligations, making the feedback more granular than the student’s step and harder to interpret. This mismatch is difficult to solve through the Lean backbone alone. Complementary methods, such as sampling counterexamples or using an LLM to generate higher-level pedagogical and tutor-like feedback, can help produce more useful explanations (formal verification could also be used to check whether the LLM generated feedback before showing it to users).






The second limitation is that 
Lean may not follow the same strategic trace as human intuition
. In our study, students found the system useful for narrowing down local issues, but less able to guide them toward the right overall strategy. When a student followed an unproductive path, several mathematically correct steps could appear before the first incorrect step; the system flagged only the incorrect step, leaving the student to identify where the proof had diverged strategically. This reflects a mismatch between formal verification and human proof reasoning: Lean and search-based provers do not necessarily follow the intuitive order in which humans understand a proof, and may produce proofs that are counterintuitive or difficult to read 
(
Shi et al., 2025b
)
. Strategic hint generation, such as tree-search-based methods studied in existing tutoring systems, could therefore complement the formal verification backbone.






Together, what FVCR systems can provide and where they are limited offers guidance for future co-reasoning tool designers on when to use an FVCR system. It also suggests that, when using a formal verification system as the backbone, task-specific auxiliary components can add useful “meat” around formal verification, varying by domain and interaction need.






Figure 12. 
This figure compares two inspection scenarios: a general inspection scenario and inspection in an FVCR system. In the general scenario, users must inspect both interpretation and execution; in an FVCR system, the emphasis is primarily on inspecting interpretation.








9.4. 
Open design challenges: faithfulness checking and auto-detecting contextual granularity




One open design challenge is 
faithfulness checking
.
In figure 
12
, we summarize users’ inspection of a collaborative system into two categories (1) inspecting whether the system’s interpretation of the presented task is faithful, and (2) inspecting whether the system’s execution matches the user’s intent, which could be correspond to gulf of execution and evaluation 
(
Norman, 2013
)
. We view inspection in FVCR systems as a special case of this broader inspection problem, one that emphasizes (1) while placing less burden on (2).






In LeanSide, the side-by-side comparison between user input and system interpretation in the informalization panel makes faithfulness inspection explicit. The open design challenge is how to make these checks lightweight enough to avoid tedious interaction, while still keeping them visible enough to hold users’ attention.






We observed that students paid more attention to steps marked gray with error messages than to steps marked green, they did not always check whether the system had correctly interpreted what they meant in each sentence before everything is green.






To address this issue, our current design requires users to click “this is what I meant” or “not what I meant” for every informalized cell before submitting the assignment. If a user clicks “not what I meant,” the step returns to gray and the student must clarify and re-verify the proof. However, this design has limitations. Students usually checked every step only after resolving all error messages and preparing to submit the assignment. As a result, participants sometimes ignored unfaithful interpretations during intermediate iterations. However, an unfaithful earlier step could prevent later causally related steps from being verified, increasing the likelihood of inaccurate judgments and error messages for the later step. This is one reason participants became stuck or moved in the wrong direction, as discussed in Section 
8.3
.






We considered two alternative designs. First, after each verification, the system could require students to confirm “this is what I meant” or “not what I meant” before showing indicators and error messages. However, because informalizations often differ from the student’s original wording even when they are faithful, this interaction could become tedious. In addition, if a student clicked “not what I meant,” the system would need to regenerate the Lean interpretation, adding waiting time while leaving open the possibility that the new interpretation would still be unfaithful. Second, similar to existing LLM interfaces, the system could ask follow-up questions when the student’s input is ambiguous. We implemented this feature in the interface shown in Figure 
13
, but because it adds complexity beyond the scope of the present study, we leave its evaluation to future work.






Another open design challenge is 
auto-detecting contextual granularity
. Human users, such as students, often learn the acceptable granularity of reasoning from surrounding context, including lectures, peer discussion, and grading expectations, without anyone stating it explicitly. By contrast, LeanSide required substantial effort to construct a mini-lemma library that encoded this granularity, through rubric lemmas and side lemmas. Even with an automated pipeline, experts still had to inspect whether the specified granularity was appropriate. In mathematics education, this granularity is relatively visible because rubrics exist for each problem; in many other reasoning tasks, it may be far more implicit. A key open challenge for co-reasoning systems is therefore how they can learn the user’s expected granularity for communicating reasoning.






Figure 13. 
Follow up questions asked by the system when a student’s step is ambiguous










10. 
Limitations




This study has several limitations. First, the participant population was relatively homogeneous: all participants were recruited from the same university, and many were majoring in Computer Science, Mathematics, or related fields. This composition was partly a consequence of the course in which we deployed the system. Although none of the participants had prior experience with Lean, they may have been more familiar with formal verification than the general population and therefore more inclined to trust the verification results. In addition, their disciplinary training may have helped them express informal reasoning more precisely, making their inputs less ambiguous than those of general users.






Second, the problems selected for this study represent only a limited subset of mathematical reasoning, focusing primarily on Linear Algebra and Optimization. This choice was motivated by two factors: (1) the deployment course focused on Linear Algebra, and (2) the current auto-formalization and prover modules perform more reliably in these domains. Consequently, the observed results may not generalize to other areas of mathematics, where users may exhibit different input behaviors and where the system may face additional challenges.

6. Discussion 
6.1. Mobility advantages are organizationally situated 
Research on scientific mobility has established that internationally mobile scientists often publish more, 
receive greater recognition, and maintain more international collaborations (Cruz-Castro & Sanz-Menéndez, 
2010; Jonkers & Cruz-Castro, 2013). More recent work has provided more contextualized interpretations by 
showing that mobility outcomes depend on career trajectories, organizational contexts, and the networks 
through which scientists access knowledge (Benz & Larivière, 2025; Chen et al., 2025). Capponi and Frenken 
(2025) similarly demonstrate that the consequences of academic training depend on the institutional and 
intellectual context in which training occurs. Our findings extend this contextual turn from mobility 
trajectories to destination-system structure. Foreign-trained faculty contribute disproportionately to highly 

 
20 
cited U.S. research, but citation differences narrow sharply when faculty are compared within the same 
institution, domain, rank, and year. At the same time, differences in publication volume and mixed-training-
origin collaboration remain. Thus, the foreign-training advantage contains two analytically distinct 
components: differential placement within the research system and differences that persist within comparable 
organizational settings. 
This distinction modifies how mobility premiums should be interpreted. Organizational position is not merely 
a confounder separating foreign training from its “net” effect. Internationally trained researchers enter a highly 
stratified destination system, and their observed contribution partly reflects where that system places them. The 
meaningful objective is therefore not to detach mobility from context, but to situate it with comparable 
scientific capabilities to organizational environments. Accordingly, our study connects mobility research with 
organizational cumulative advantage and academic hierarchy (Clauset et al., 2015; Wapman et al., 2022; Way 
et al., 2019). 
6.2. International mobility carries relational capital, not simply additional ties 
The collaboration network results expand the literature on the benefit of having elevated scientific networks. 
Existing literature found migrant and return scientists possess larger international networks and international 
connections can constitute scientific social capital by providing access to foreign knowledge and collaborators 
(Franzoni et al., 2014; Scellato et al., 2015).  Our results add a different dimension: foreign-trained faculty not 
only have greater prior collaborator reach and breadth, they also received higher return on elite output because 
of their wider collaboration compared with U.S.-trained faculty. This pattern is stable across alternative 
network windows and broadly similar across scientific domains. The result extends the literature from network 
possession to the relationship between network position and subsequent scientific performance. 
That distinction matters for social capital. Our evidence suggests that the relationship between connectivity and 
scientific output depends partly on the trajectory through which that connectivity was accumulated. One 
possibility, consistent with Scellato et al. (2015), is that networks spanning training systems contain 
complementary or less redundant resources. The heterogeneity across terminal-degree countries reinforces this 
point. Our country results showed substantial variation in the network–output relationship across training 
systems. Such systems may differ in their connectivity to U.S. science, institutional pathways, and migration 
selectivity. International training should therefore be understood as a heterogeneous source of relational 
capital.  
6.3. Mobility and knowledge recombination 
A third explanation links mobility to knowledge recombination. International mobility exposes scientists to 
new research environments, collaborators, and ideas, potentially enabling exploration beyond established 
knowledge bases. A recent study has shown that mobility increased research quality alongside collaboration 
with new, higher-quality coauthors and exploration of new topics (Baruffaldi et al., 2020), which complements 
broader research linking novel knowledge combinations to scientific impact (Uzzi et al., 2013).  
Our results place an important boundary on this explanation. Foreign-trained faculty appear cognitively 
broader in raw comparisons, but this difference disappears once the larger size of their prior publication 
portfolios is considered. Their distinctive collaboration reach therefore does not translate into correspondingly 
broader individual topic portfolios. 
This separation of social reach from cognitive breadth suggests that access to heterogeneous knowledge may 
instead be organized through collaborators. In this sense, our findings complement the recombination 
argument, which suggests that one consequence of international training may reside in the social distribution of 
knowledge across relationships, rather than in greater cognitive diversification within individual portfolios 
(Wang, 2016). 
 
21 
6.4. International training as a feature of scientific capacity 
These results connect literatures that have largely examined different parts of the same process. Mobility 
research has established that scientists carry knowledge and relationships across borders (Cruz-Castro & Sanz-
Menéndez, 2010; Edler et al., 2011; Franzoni et al., 2014; Jonkers & Cruz-Castro, 2013; Scellato et al., 2015). 
Research on scientific careers shows that the consequences of mobility and training depend on trajectories and 
contexts (Baruffaldi & Landoni, 2012; Baruffaldi et al., 2020; Benz & Larivière, 2025). Network research, 
meanwhile, shows that access to international connections can affect scientific performance (Chen et al., 
2025). Our study brings these arguments together at the level of the destination research system. Its principal 
contribution is to show that international training is associated with three separable features of scientific 
capacity: organizational structure, collaboration networks, and research portfolio.  
6.5. Limitations and future research 
Foreign-trained faculty employed at U.S. universities are selected through training, migration, hiring, and 
career progression, while network position is itself shaped by prior productivity, reputation, resources, and 
scientific specialization. The analyses identify organizational and relational patterns, not selection mechanisms 
of foreign-trained faculty into U.S. universities or causal effects of foreign training or collaborator reach. 
Terminal-degree location captures only one element of mobility history. Studies showed the importance of 
using complete career trajectories in measuring mobility effect (Benz & Larivière, 2025) and the stage at 
which international movement occurs is related to subsequent network structure (Scellato et al., 2015). Future 
research should therefore reconstruct sequences of doctoral training, postdoctoral mobility, institutional 
movement, and international collaboration. Last, coauthorship captures only publication ties and does not 
reveal other relationships such as mentorship or tacit knowledge transfer. These constraints provide boundaries 
of the interpretations of the obtained results.

Conclusion




This paper is a diagnostic study of LLM robustness to numerical claim perturbations. Standard fine-tuning teaches the model to confirm a claim’s surface form rather than verify it against evidence, and accuracy on label-flipping inputs collapses to single digits. Adversarial fine-tuning on counterfactual examples recovers near-perfect accuracy, with small QLoRA-tuned models (0.6B–8B) surpassing zero-shot 32B and frontier closed-source baselines on the hardest perturbations. Composition matters more than variety: 
Masked
 and 
Numeration
 are essential, 
Approximation
 and 
Random
 redundant. Robustness also transfers across languages and domains without target-language data, suggesting a generalised numerical decision boundary rather than memorised edits.










Limitations




Data and perturbation scope.




Our perturbation taxonomy rewrites numerical expressions in the claim while leaving evidence unchanged. Section 
5.7
 reaches the evidence side through VitaminC’s human-authored revisions, but our generator does not produce them, and jointly perturbing claim and evidence remains an open direction. The six types focus on scalar quantities as digits or written-out numbers, so robustness to unit conversions, date arithmetic, compound quantities, or numbers in tables is not guaranteed. Training and primary evaluation use QuanTemp (English fact-checking); cross-dataset experiments add Spanish, AVeriTeC and VitaminC but remain in English and Spanish and, apart from VitaminC’s single-sentence evidence, within the fact-checking domain, so broader language coverage and generalisation to scientific, financial, or tabular settings both require further evaluation.








Model and evaluation setup.




Experiments use only the Qwen3 family (0.6B–32B) with QLoRA and soft prompt tuning. 
Aarnes and Setty (2025)
 document the same numerical brittleness on LLaMA-family models, so we expect the qualitative findings to hold across LLaMA, Mistral, Gemma, and comparable open families, though confirming this directly is left for future work; quantitative effects (the scale at which diminishing returns set in, the size of the QLoRA-vs.-soft-prompt gap) may shift across families and PEFT methods. The soft-prompt baseline reuses QLoRA hyperparameters, making it a matched-budget rather than optimally tuned comparison. All experiments assume gold evidence, isolating verification from retrieval; whether the robustness gains survive noisy or incomplete retrieval is left for future work.








Interpretability.




We lack a mechanistic account of 
why
 adversarial fine-tuning works. It is unclear whether models learn to attend more carefully to numerical tokens, develop surface-form-invariant representations, or rely on other signals; attribution, probing, and activation-patching analyses would be needed to explain the gains and anticipate failure modes — a direction we intend to pursue.










Ethical Considerations




This work studies the robustness of LLMs used for numerical claim verification. We identify specific weaknesses that existing models exhibit when claims contain perturbed numerical expressions, and we show that adversarial fine-tuning substantially reduces these vulnerabilities. We do not endorse any specific model or configuration for deployment in real-world fact-checking pipelines; fact-checking is a nuanced task where model outputs should be treated as decision-support tools rather than authoritative verdicts, and human oversight remains essential.






The perturbation techniques studied could, in principle, be used to craft adversarial claims that evade automated fact-checkers. We consider this a reason to publish rather than withhold the findings: understanding and documenting these failure modes is a prerequisite for building more resilient systems, and the perturbation types we study are straightforward enough that they are already available to any motivated adversary. All data used in this work is sourced from publicly available fact-checking corpora, and no personal or sensitive information is involved.

Conclusions and Future Work




We introduced a simple logical framework for norm-guided decision making under uncertainty.
Starting from a restricted fragment of Chellas’ Minimal Deontic Logic, we identified a language
where deontic reasoning reduces to classical propositional reasoning while retaining obligations
and prohibitions over atomic actions. We extended this fragment with explicitly represented
conditional norms and factual detachment, obtaining a lightweight deontic logic.






To reason under incomplete information, we combined the framework with multi-agent doxastic logic,
allowing norms to depend on agents’ beliefs and beliefs about norms. We introduced the Doxastic
Norm Compliance Optimization Problem (DNCOP), where an agent selects decisions minimizing weighted
norm violations. By distinguishing optimization relative to the agent’s beliefs from optimization
relative to the objective state of the world, the framework captures a key aspect of autonomous
decision making under uncertainty. We identified locality and truthfulness conditions under which
these perspectives coincide, guaranteeing that subjectively optimal decisions are also objectively
optimal.






The framework also admits efficient computation. For local, decision-sound DNCOPs, we showed that
optimal decisions can be found by a polynomial-time reduction to weighted partial MaxSAT,
leveraging mature optimization techniques while preserving logical rigour and transparency.






The framework deliberately favors simplicity over expressiveness. Restricting normative contents to
atomic propositions enables reductions to propositional reasoning and straightforward integration
with epistemic formalisms, while still covering a broad range of practical decision-making
scenarios. Its modular design leaves room for richer normative and epistemic extensions.

15

Another promising direction is to study decentralized settings in which multiple agents make

One of the most established laws in Physics is the exponential decay law. It is derived at a phenomenological level under the assumption that past events cannot influence the decay rate. title: Comparison of Common Crawl News & GDELT
hypothesis: This paper directly compares GDELT and CC-News, two publicly available and widely used news datasets. Analyzing each dataset, we seek to compare GDELT and CC-News while highlighting their strengths and limitations.
conclusion:
Conclusion and Future Work




In an era where data plays a pivotal role in shaping decisions, solving problems, and advancing systems, the storage and accessibility of information are paramount. Web archiving fosters innovation and academic research in our digital age. However, many web archives are limited due to restricted public access or technological and copyright constraints. The GDELT project and Common Crawl have emerged as pioneers, offering extensive, freely available big data that contributes significantly to the academic community.






This paper presents a comparative analysis of two prominent news datasets: GDELT and CC-News. Our research examines various aspects of each dataset, including size, diversity, news source quality, and language distribution. Through this exploration, we provided beneficial insights to the computational journalism and social science communities. Researchers should weigh the distinct characteristics of these datasets when selecting datasets for their studies.






To conclude, GDELT, with its collection spanning traditional news sources worldwide, presents a comprehensive and diverse range of information within its news data. On the other hand, CC-News, derived from the Common Crawl, offers a higher volume of news data and provides a perspective on other web-based news content. We found the largest differences between the two datasets in their news sources. Furthermore, our comparative analysis highlights the strengths and limitations of each dataset, allowing researchers to make informed choices based on their specific study requirements, not limited to utilizing both datasets simultaneously to leverage the unique characteristics of each fully.






In future work, we will classify news articles by topic to better analyze the composition of the content of each dataset. It would also be helpful to understand how the emergence of large language models increases the value of these types of datasets and may limit their availability (for example, increasing numbers of news websites block CC-Bot). As the value of these types of datasets increases, understanding the nuanced differences between them becomes important. Our work takes a step toward exploring these differences.

When trained on disjointed datasets sharing only a single anchor modality, these models successfully generalised to novel modality combinations, maintaining robust predictive performance even when the highly informative FLAIR sequence was unavailable.






Additionally, we address a major hurdle in clinical deployment: silent data degradation. By introducing the Multimodal Attention Router (MMAR) block alongside a complimentary corruption augmentation strategy, we showed that this proof-of-concept method can dynamically adapt to unflagged, catastrophically corrupted modalities. Through spatially adaptive feature routing, the MMAR-based model learns to treat severely degraded regions in scans as missing, preserving segmentation accuracy in the presence of extreme noise, bias fields, and false-present modalities.






Ultimately, these strategies offer a robust and practical pathway for developing and deploying medical image segmentation tools in imperfect, real-world clinical environments.






Limitations




We acknowledge several limitations in this study.
First, it is likely that our comparative results are highly sensitive to the total volume and modality distribution of the training data; we urge caution when extrapolating our results to other data distributions.
Second, due to the number of individual training runs required and limited computational resources, our evaluations are centred on a single random training, validation, and test split, and each model was trained only once. While we attempted to mitigate the impact of these factors by performing statistical significance tests, we must highlight this limitation.
Third, our evaluation relies solely on the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC). Although DSC has known limitations, it remains the standard segmentation metric and correlates strongly with other measures. Since our primary objective was the relative comparison of methods rather than establishing absolute task performance, limiting our evaluation to DSC allowed us to reduce the complexity of the results while preserving statistical power.
Fourth, due to a lack of truly corrupted scans in our dataset, test time corruption transformations were required for evaluating the models that were trained for corruption-robustness, using corruption augmentation. To mitigate this bias, we applied different transformation parameters during training and testing augmentations.
Finally, because our primary motivation was to evaluate the viability of hetero-modal learning in data-starved clinical scenarios, we opted for foundational, proven baseline methods. However, an abundance of complex architectures and training techniques have been proposed for imbalanced hetero-modal learning—typically evaluated on the BraTS brain tumour dataset 
(
Menze et al., 2014
)
. We leave a systematic benchmarking of these methods applied to WMH and ISL segmentation for future work.

title: Is Weight Tying Still Beneficial for Decoder-Only LLMs in Private Settings Under DP-SGD?
hypothesis: By avoiding per-example gradient materialization, Ghost Clipping dramatically reduces GPU memory consumption while preserving the clipping behavior of DP-SGD. However, its norm computation relies on the assumption that layer-wise gradient contributions can be decomposed independently and summed additively.
conclusion:
Conclusion




This paper investigated the interaction between DP-SGD, ghost clipping, and weight tying in decoder-only language models. Through theoretical analysis and extensive experiments on GPT2 and DistilGPT2, we showed that the benefits of weight tying observed in standard non-private training do not naturally transfer to the differentially private setting. Across both models, untied embeddings consistently achieved superior privacy–utility–efficiency trade-offs, improving predictive performance and optimization stability while preserving the substantial memory savings provided by ghost clipping.






A key contribution is identifying a limitation of ghost clipping under tied embeddings. We show that weight tying introduces an interaction term in the per-sample gradient norm, violating the additive separability assumption used in ghost norm computation. Consequently, treating the two pathway contributions as independent parameter blocks omits their cross-term and does not recover the exact norm of the shared parameter.
Although exact norms can be restored by including the missing cross-term, this requires materializing gradient interactions, which ghost clipping aims to avoid.






Taken together, these findings demonstrate that scalable differentially private optimization is not fully architecture-agnostic. Its correctness depends on how architectural choices shape gradient structure. Ghost clipping remains exact and effective when parameters are disjoint, but tied embeddings violate its assumptions. This highlights the need to jointly design model architectures and privacy-preserving optimization methods for efficient private foundation models.

Motivated by practical issues with implementation of IPEA, a popular iterative algorithm well suited for for phase estimation on NISQ and early FT hardware, we consider the problem of allocation of number of shots across iterations. Particularly relevant are the so-called economic models of territoriality, which evaluate optimal balances between benefits and costs under the assumption that behaviors affecting an animal’s fitness have been shaped by natural selection, thus linking territorial behavior to Optimal Foraging Theory

Our results show that the interplay between energetic constraints, spatial connectivity, and individual competition strongly shapes territorial organization in systems of competing males. Using an individual-based spatial model, we show how these factors jointly regulate the persistence of males, the distribution of territory sizes, and the emergence of unequal territorial structures (see a schematic representation of our results in Fig. 
10
). Although the model considers a single species and only intraspecific competition, the results reveal mechanisms that resemble patterns predicted by broader ecological theories of competition and coexistence.






In classical Lotka-Volterra competition models and in Modern Coexistence Theory, coexistence among competitors is expected when intraspecific competition is stronger than interspecific competition. However, these approaches are typically phenomenological and summarize competitive interactions through simple terms such as 
1
/
K

i

, 
38
]
. In contrast, our individual-based model generates a comparable stabilizing effect through explicit energetic confrontation costs between individuals. These costs limit territorial expansion and prevent the progressive exclusion of competitors, ultimately stabilizing both the number of males and the distribution of territories. Moreover, the model allows us to explore how these competitive costs interact with other ecological factors, such as resource distribution and spatial connectivity.






Landscape connectivity emerges in our simulations as a key factor shaping the outcome of territorial competition. Connectivity, understood here as the structural continuity between resource patches, has long been recognized as an important determinant of ecosystem functioning and species persistence 
[
41
, 
18
]
. In our model, connectivity is controlled by the seeds propagation parameter 
α
\alpha
, which determines how resources spread across the matrix. Different levels of connectivity generate markedly different territorial outcomes: highly connected matrices promote strong competition and the exclusion of many males, whereas fragmented resource distributions allow more individuals to maintain territories. This shows that simple changes in spatial structure can produce non-linear effects on population organization.






From this perspective, matrix connectivity may play a role similar to that proposed by disturbance-based coexistence mechanisms. Reduced connectivity can create spatial refuges that limit direct interactions between dominant and subordinate individuals, allowing smaller or less competitive males to maintain territories. In this sense, spatial fragmentation can operate analogously to the Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis at the intraspecific level, preventing the monopolization of resources by a few dominant individuals 
[
17
, 
61
]
. However, this mechanism must be interpreted in conjunction with energetic constraints, since body size strongly affects locomotion costs according to the allometric relationship described by Taylor and Heglund 
[
66
]
.






The model also reveals interesting parallels with systems studied in econophysics. In simulations without confrontation costs, the number of males declines continuously while the distribution of territorial areas converges toward a stable configuration. Similar dynamics have been observed in economic exchange models, where interactions among agents lead to stable but highly unequal wealth distributions 
[
55
, 
19
, 
29
]
. Such analogies contribute to a growing body of research exploring conceptual links between ecological and economic systems, particularly in terms of resource allocation and competition among agents 
[
62
, 
7
, 
68
]
.






Territorial organization also has important implications for population structure and reproductive dynamics. In wild camelids, territorial males defend resource-rich areas in order to attract and retain females. Consequently, variation in territory size may translate into differences in reproductive success, survival, and ultimately genetic contribution to future generations 
[
26
, 
76
, 
3
, 
56
]
. Our results suggest that highly connected and energetically rich environments tend to concentrate resources into fewer territories, potentially reducing genetic diversity by increasing reproductive inequality among males. Conversely, stronger confrontation costs tend to favor the persistence of more males with positive balances, and therefore stable territories, and a more distributed reproductive structure.






These findings complement previous theoretical work on the social organization of wild camelids. In a previous study we had analyzed how female distribution emerges from the interaction between territory quality, male performance, and the presence of bachelor males in the system 
[
31
]
. Combining both approaches suggests that highly productive and well-connected environments may generate social contexts where many males fail to secure territories and instead adopt harassment strategies. Under these conditions, females may prefer to form larger groups despite the potential costs associated with resource competition within groups. Such dynamics can further increase inequality in the distribution of females among territories, adding another layer of complexity to the system.






Our modeling approach is also related to economic models of animal territoriality, which interpret territorial behavior as the outcome of cost–benefit optimization strategies. Many of these models assume that individuals adjust their behavior to maximize energetic benefits relative to costs affecting fitness 
[
53
, 
21
, 
3
, 
35
, 
36
]
. However, most of these models are deterministic, non-spatial, and focus on the decision-making process of a single territorial resident. In contrast, our model explicitly incorporates spatial structure and the simultaneous interaction of multiple competing males, allowing the emergent territorial configuration to arise from decentralized individual decisions.






Another important component of our model is the explicit incorporation of allometric constraints. Locomotion costs associated with territorial patrol depend strongly on body mass and biomechanical limitations. These energetic costs ultimately influence the size and stability of territories, linking individual physiological traits with population-level spatial organization 
[
63
, 
11
, 
15
, 
9
]
. In this sense, the energetic balance framework provides a mechanistic bridge between individual traits and emergent social structures.






Finally, it is important to compare our model outcomes with empirical observations. In wild camelids, typical territory sizes range between approximately 13 and 46 hectares 
[
42
, 
76
, 
5
, 
64
]

In real systems, several ecological factors (that are not included in the model) may constrain territorial expansion, including selective grazing, habitat visibility, predation risk, and interactions with other members of the family group. Nevertheless, large territories have been reported in some guanaco populations, reaching between 200 and 900 hectares in certain contexts 
[
48
]
.






Regarding energetic inputs, the main grasses consumed by wild camelids belong to genera such as 
Stipa
, 
Poa
 and 
Panicum

However, real males must share these resources with females and offspring and also incur additional energetic costs associated with social monitoring, territorial defense, and interactions with bachelor males 
[
8
, 
58

57
, 
40
, 
32
, 
65
, 
50
, 
49
, 
31
]

In summary, our study illustrates how territorial organization can emerge from the interaction between energetic constraints, spatial structure and individual competition. By explicitly linking allometric scaling to competitive dynamics, the framework provides a mechanistic perspective connecting individual physiology to population-level patterns. Beyond camelids, these results suggest that incorporating energetic and spatial constraints into models of territoriality may be essential for understanding the diversity and stability of social systems in vertebrates.

Abstract


Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems remains a challenge for Low-Resource Languages (LRLs), where standard reference-based metrics fall short. This paper investigates the viability of the "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm for Romanian by adapting the Ragas framework using next-generation models (Gemini 2.5 and Gemini 3). By leveraging these newer, more powerful models, we aim to establish a robust baseline for automated RAG evaluation in Romanian, providing a transferable strategy for other low-resource languages.

This study bridges a gap in the evaluation of RAG systems for Low-Resource Languages. By introducing 
AdminRo-Eval
 and benchmarking three automated evaluation strategies, we demonstrated that English-centric metrics cannot be blindly transferred to Romanian without performance degradation.






Our experiments reveal that the "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm is viable for Romanian, provided the methodology is tailored to the specific metric. We found that the granular decomposition of the Ragas framework is superior for objective metrics like 
Faithfulness
 (96% alignment with Gemini 2.5 Pro), whereas Comparative Ranking is more effective for nuanced semantic judgments like 
Answer Relevance
 (90% alignment). Furthermore, our results caution against the use of lightweight "Flash" models for complex reasoning tasks in LRLs, as evidenced by their inability to accurately assess Context Relevance. Ultimately, while newer models like Gemini 3 Pro excel in specific areas, the older Gemini 2.5 Pro architecture provided the most robust and consistent baseline for Romanian RAG evaluation.






To further advance RAG evaluation for under-represented languages, we propose to expand the AdminRo-Eval dataset beyond public administration to include medical and legal domains, where hallucination risks carry higher stakes. Such observations will provide stronger constraints on the evolutionary pathway from vertically extended Class 0 disks to the thin dust layers commonly observed in Class II systems. magnetic configuration. The coexistence of structural stability, localized Ce  4f magnetism, and

)

McConvey and Guha, 2024
)
. Our findings show that fairness interventions, confined to the narrow space vendor control permits, can become instruments of that consolidation rather than checks on it. The eagle casts for prey; the poet and scientist cast for word and idea. Neurons wander through tissue, holding out for just the right synaptic partners to make us,
